title: Geospatial Data Analysis

Lecture pages for GDA. Each page mixes short explanations, R code you can copy into RStudio, and interactive figures you can explore on your own.
Canvas remains the official home for the syllabus, assignments, and grades.

Lectures

title: Coordinate Reference Systems
text:
In your homework, two layers that should have overlapped didn’t. Something failed loudly, something failed silently, or both. Today is about why, so that you can spot the problem in any data and in any code an AI writes for you.
By the end of this session you should be able to:

Tell a geographic CRS from a projected one by reading R’s printout.
Explain what a datum is and when a datum difference matters.
Explain why every flat map distorts something, and choose a projection that protects what your analysis measures.
Use EPSG codes to name, check, and convert CRSs in R.

title: Coordinate Reference Systems
text:
1 The failure, again
We’ll use small datasets that come with terra: elevation for Luxembourg and the country’s 12 cantons (districts). Both arrive in longitude and latitude.

library(sf)       # vector data
library(terra)    # raster data
library(dplyr)    # filter() and friends
library(spData)   # the `world` dataset, used in section 4
library(units)    # converting m^2 to km^2, used in section 4

Warning: package 'units' was built under R version 4.2.3



# Elevation raster for Luxembourg
elev_file <- system.file("ex/elev.tif", package = "terra")
elev <- rast(elev_file)

# The 12 cantons of Luxembourg, as sf polygons
cantons_file <- system.file("ex/lux.shp", package = "terra")
cantons <- st_read(cantons_file)

Reading layer `lux' from data source 
  `C:\Users\alonzo\AppData\Local\R\win-library\4.2\terra\ex\lux.shp' using driver `ESRI Shapefile'
Simple feature collection with 12 features and 6 fields
Geometry type: POLYGON
Dimension:     XY
Bounding box:  xmin: 5.74414 ymin: 49.44781 xmax: 6.528252 ymax: 50.18162
Geodetic CRS:  WGS 84


To set up the problem, imagine Luxembourg’s mapping agency sends you the elevation data in their national grid, EPSG:2169. We’ll create that version here. (project() converts a raster between CRSs. We’ll look at its options in a later session.)

elev_lux <- project(elev, "EPSG:2169")
elev_lux

class       : SpatRaster 
dimensions  : 108, 74, 1  (nrow, ncol, nlyr)
resolution  : 771.9464, 771.9464  (x, y)
extent      : 49072.34, 106196.4, 56455.27, 139825.5  (xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax)

min value   :  141.4412 
max value   :  543.9387 








TipPredict



Compare the extent of elev_lux above with the Bounding box that st_read() printed for cantons. If we draw the cantons on top of the elevation, what will we see?



# Raster first, cantons on top in red
plot(elev_lux)
plot(st_geometry(cantons), add = TRUE, border = "red")








No red lines, no error, no warning. Now two geoprocessing steps:

# Loud failure: crop() checks that the layers overlap, and stops
crop(elev_lux, cantons)

Error:
! [crop] extents do not overlap



# Silent failure: a mean elevation for each canton... all NaN
# (na.rm = TRUE is needed because elev.tif has no-data cells along the border)
bad <- extract(elev_lux, cantons, fun = mean, na.rm = TRUE)
bad

Hold on to these three symptoms. The rest of the session explains them, and in section 6 we fix them.

title: Coordinate Reference Systems
Coordinate Reference Systems
text:
3 Datums and ellipsoids
Latitude and longitude only mean something once you say which model of the Earth they’re measured on.

The Earth is close to an ellipsoid: a sphere squashed at the poles. The equatorial radius is about 21 km longer than the polar radius.
An ellipsoid is the mathematical shape (its size and flattening).
A datum is an ellipsoid plus how it is pinned to the real Earth: where its center is and how it’s oriented.

Change the datum and the same coordinates point to a slightly different spot on the ground.









Datum
Ellipsoid
Pinned to
Where you’ll meet it




NAD27
Clarke 1866
A survey point in Kansas (Meades Ranch)
Old maps and surveys


NAD83
GRS 80
Earth’s center (fixed to the North American plate)
US Census / TIGER data, state agencies


WGS 84
WGS 84
Earth’s center (global)
GPS, most web data, EPA TRI



Let’s measure how much a datum matters. Take one set of coordinates for the AU campus and label it with two datums:

# One pair of numbers: longitude, latitude
au_xy <- st_point(c(-77.0887, 38.9365))

# The same numbers, labeled with two different datums
au_nad27 <- st_sfc(au_xy, crs = 4267)
au_nad83 <- st_sfc(au_xy, crs = 4269)

# Convert the NAD27 point to NAD83, so both are on one datum
au_nad27_converted <- st_transform(au_nad27, 4269)

# How far apart are "the same" coordinates on the ground?
st_distance(au_nad83, au_nad27_converted)

Units: [m]
         [,1]
[1,] 28.71194


About 28 meters, which is enough to put a facility on the wrong side of a street or a census tract boundary. Between NAD83 and WGS 84, the difference in the US is only about a meter or two. That rarely matters for tract-level analysis or 30 m rasters.
But R can’t know what precision your question needs, so it treats any difference in CRS as a mismatch. That’s why, in the asthma problem, the EPA TRI points (WGS 84) still have to be transformed before they can be joined to the Census tracts (NAD83).






NoteBehind the scenes: datum shifts need extra files





Accurate NAD27 → NAD83 conversion uses a grid of measured shifts. That grid is a separate download, not built into R. If PROJ (the library under sf and terra) can’t find it, it falls back to a “ballpark” conversion. That can mean no shift at all, with no error. This page was built with sf_proj_network(TRUE), which lets PROJ fetch grids from the internet as needed. You’ll rarely need NAD27 in this course. The lesson is the general one: a step that runs without error isn’t proof that it did what you think.

5 EPSG codes: names for CRSs
Saying “NAD83, Lambert Conformal Conic, standard parallels 38.3° and 39.45°, meters” every time would be painful. The EPSG registry (now maintained by IOGP, the oil and gas producers’ association) gives each complete CRS definition a number. One code bundles the datum, the ellipsoid, the projection and its parameters, and the units.
Codes you’ll meet in this course:










EPSG
Name
Type
Units
Where you’ll see it

WGS 84
Geographic
degrees

NAD83

degrees

NAD27
Geographic
degrees

WGS 84 / Pseudo-Mercator
Projected, cylindrical
“meters” (stretched)
Web map tiles. Display only.

Projected, conic, equal-area
meters

NAD83 / UTM zone 18N
Projected, transverse Mercator
meters
Distances in DC, MD, VA

NAD83 / Maryland
Projected, Lambert conic
meters

2248
NAD83 / Maryland (ftUS)
Projected, Lambert conic
US feet
Maryland county GIS. Check the units!



You don’t need to memorize these. You need to know how to read one. Ask terra for a short description, or print the full definition with sf:

# Short summary: name, code, and where it's meant to be used
crs("EPSG:26985", describe = TRUE)

TipChoose a CRS



For each task, pick a CRS from the table and defend it in one sentence.

Total impervious area in each Maryland county.
Number of TRI facilities within 1 km of each census tract centroid in Baltimore.
Asthma prevalence compared across all 48 contiguous states.
An interactive web map for a community group.









NoteSome defensible answers






5070 (equal-area) or 26985. Within one state, State Plane’s area distortion is tiny, so either is defensible. Saying why is the point.
26985 or 26918: both are in meters and accurate locally for distance. Not 4326: a 1 km buffer needs meters.
5070: equal-area across the whole country.
3857 for display. Do the analysis in a measuring CRS first, then transform for the map.

title: Coordinate Reference Systems
section: 6 Back to the failure: fix it and check it
text:
6 Back to the failure: fix it and check it
Now the symptoms from section 1 make sense:

The cantons’ coordinates are around 6 and 50 (degrees). The raster’s are in the tens of thousands (meters).
plot() just draws numbers. It put the cantons in a tiny patch near x = 6, y = 50, far outside the raster’s extent, so nothing appeared on the map.
crop() compared the two extents, found no overlap, and stopped.
extract() found no raster cells inside any polygon and returned NaN, without complaint.

The fix is to put both layers in one CRS. Transform the vector to match the raster, not the other way around. Moving polygon vertices is exact, while reprojecting a raster has to resample cell values.

# Convert the cantons into the raster's CRS
cantons_lux <- st_transform(cantons, crs(elev_lux))

# Check 1: do the two CRSs now match?
st_crs(cantons_lux) == st_crs(elev_lux)

[1] TRUE

# Check 2: are the coordinate ranges now comparable?
st_bbox(cantons_lux)

     xmin      ymin      xmax      ymax 
 49540.31  57009.53 105922.01 138631.13 

ext(elev_lux)

SpatExtent : 49072.3397901184, 106196.374340225, 56455.2689687042, 139825.481555346 (xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax)



# Check 3: look at it
plot(elev_lux)
plot(st_geometry(cantons_lux), add = TRUE, border = "red")









# The zonal mean now works: one number per canton
good <- extract(elev_lux, cantons_lux, fun = mean, na.rm = TRUE)
cantons_lux$elev_mean <- good$elevation

# Check 4: no missing values, and plausible elevations (meters)
sum(is.na(cantons_lux$elev_mean))

[1] 0

summary(cantons_lux$elev_mean)

   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
  239.6   312.9   322.3   339.7   374.2   467.1 








WarningLabeling is not converting



st_transform() converts coordinates: the numbers change. st_set_crs() (or st_crs(x) <- ...) only relabels them: the numbers stay the same. Relabeling is correct only when a file has no CRS and you know what it should be. AI assistants sometimes suggest it as a “fix” for a mismatch. Here’s what that does:

# Wrong: claims the degrees are now meters
cantons_relabeled <- st_set_crs(cantons, 2169)

Warning: st_crs<- : replacing crs does not reproject data; use st_transform for that

st_bbox(cantons_relabeled)

     xmin      ymin      xmax      ymax 
 5.744140 49.447807  6.528252 50.181622 


R warns you, and the bounding box gives it away: the “meters” are still 5.7 to 50.2. In EPSG:2169, coordinates that small sit at the grid’s origin, which is in France, about 120 km southwest of Luxembourg’s center.

title: Coordinate Reference Systems
text:
7 In your code








Question
Function
What to look for




What CRS is this?
Print the object; st_crs(x); crs(r, describe = TRUE)
Name, EPSG code, units


Degrees or meters?
st_is_longlat(x); is.lonlat(r)
TRUE means degrees


Do my layers match?
st_crs(a) == st_crs(b); compare st_bbox() and ext()
Same CRS; ranges that overlap


Does it look right?
plot() the raster, then the vector with add = TRUE
Lines where you expect them


Convert a vector
st_transform(x, crs)
The bbox numbers change


Convert a raster
project(r, crs)
Resamples values (later session)


Label a CRS-less file
st_set_crs(x, crs)
Only when the CRS is missing and known



The habit that ties it together: check the CRS before any operation that combines two layers, and check the result after. Most CRS mistakes don’t produce errors. They produce wrong answers.

title: Coordinate Reference Systems
text:
8 Check yourself






Note1. A bounding box reads xmin: 316268 ymin: 4295630 xmax: 334407 ymax: 4318264. Degrees or meters? Projected or geographic?





Meters, so it’s projected. Longitudes only go to ±180 and latitudes to ±90. Numbers in the hundreds of thousands and millions look like UTM. (This is Washington, DC, in UTM zone 18N.)









Note2. Why did extract() return NaN instead of an error?





It did what it was asked: it looked for raster cells inside each polygon and found none, because the polygons sat far outside the raster’s extent. An empty result isn’t an error to the function. Only you know it’s wrong, which is why you check for NAs after every extract.









Note3. An AI’s code calls st_transform(tracts, 3857) before computing st_area(). What’s the problem?





Web Mercator inflates area by a factor that grows with latitude. At Maryland’s latitude (about 39° N), that’s about 1.66×, so every area would be about two-thirds too large. Use 5070 or 26985, or compute the area on the original lon/lat data.









Note4. TRI facilities are in EPSG:4326 and tracts are in EPSG:4269. The difference is about a meter. Why transform anyway?





Because sf requires both layers to have the same CRS before it will join them, and it can’t judge whether a meter matters for your question. Transform one to match the other (or both to a projected CRS you’ll measure in) and the join runs.
